This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Server orders bound for Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia are stuck after Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) withheld approval to ship them, and one Singapore cloud project tied to ByteDance has already lost some bank backing, according to a Financial Times report.

Dell (NYSE:DELL) and Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI), which build Nvidia's chips into servers, relayed the message to customers in those countries, three people familiar with the matter said.

Nvidia and its partners are figuring out how to meet the new requirements, and the people said it is unclear whether the block is short-lived.

Aolani, a Singapore cloud company, had lined up leases of computing power to ByteDance. Lenders backing the project have frozen roughly $500 million in credit, and ByteDance could walk away, two of the people said.

The pause follows Commerce Department rules issued last week to stop Chinese firms from reaching restricted chips through cloud providers. Those providers have 90 days to get a license.

Nvidia's Singapore unit booked $104 billion in revenue in 2025, up 72%, according to company accounts.

Image from Pixabay

Dell Technologies and Hewlett Packard Enterprise both reported this week. Dell ended its October quarter with a record $132.3 billion backlog of AI server orders. HPE raised its revenue growth outlook for fiscal 2027, the year ending October 2027, to a midpoint of 31%.

A backlog is orders, not cash. This article looks at the cash. On that test, Super Micro Computer has the widest gap between profit and cash of the three server makers. Over the four quarters to Sep 30, 2026, it booked $3,656 million of profit, while its business used $6,326 million of cash.

HPE is the one holding the inventory. On Jul 31, its stock of unsold goods equalled 148.7 days of its cost of sales, the most in its last 18 quarters. Yet HPE turns profit into cash best of the three. Its operating cash over four quarters was 2.4 times its net income.

How Did HPE And Dell Stock React To Their Reports?

HPE fell 16.3% on Tuesday, Nov 24, the first session after its report. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF slipped 0.49% that day. Over the two sessions since the report, HPE is down 15.0%.

Dell fell 11.8% on Tuesday. That move came before its report that evening. It rose 0.60% on Wednesday, Nov 25, to close at $297.06.

Dell closed Wednesday 50.0% below its 52-week high, even with a record AI backlog. If you are keeping cash out of the market until stocks like this settle, that cash does not have to sit idle while you wait. Here is what HPE itself said. It expects its gross margin, the share of sales left after the cost of goods, to moderate in the second half of fiscal 2027. It pointed to more AI servers in the mix and costs rising faster than prices. Its October-quarter gross margin was 38%, down 2.2 points from the quarter before.

Three numbers tell the story. Operating cash is the cash the business itself brings in. Receivable days count how long customers take to pay. Inventory days count how long goods sit before they are sold.

title: Nvidia halts chip exports to south-east Asia
detail:
Nvidia halts chip exports to south-east Asia
Tom Haynes
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 4:17 AM EST 2 min read
NVDA
DELL
SMCI
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive after pressure from Donald Trump - AFP via Getty Images

Nvidia has blocked shipments of powerful AI servers to four Asian countries as Washington cracks down on Chinese access to cutting-edge American technology.

The US chip giant has told manufacturing partners including Dell and Super Micro, which install Nvidia's chips into servers, to pause orders to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to the Financial Times.

Buyers in those countries have been informed that Nvidia will not permit these servers to be shipped, although it remains unclear whether the suspension is temporary.

The measures have been announced just days after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive under pressure from Donald Trump.

The move threatens to disrupt a data centre boom across south-east Asia, where Chinese technology companies have been renting access to powerful US chips that they cannot buy directly.

Washington has long restricted exports of Nvidia's most advanced processors to China over concerns they could strengthen Beijing's military and intelligence capabilities.

However, Chinese developers have been able to use the chips remotely by paying cloud computing businesses to operate them in countries such as Malaysia.

New US rules, which came into force on Nov 19, require licences for exports of advanced chips to the four affected countries and Brazil, with exemptions for some American-owned customers.

Data centres already providing significant computing power to restricted Chinese businesses have been given 90 days to obtain permission to continue doing so.

An executive at a cloud company told the Financial Times there was little guidance on how to apply for licences, leaving businesses uncertain about whether they could fulfil existing contracts.

The decision has left manufacturers scrambling to establish which orders can proceed.

Nikkei Asia reported last week that at least two Nvidia server suppliers had suspended deliveries to customers in the region. One had also stopped taking orders from new customers.

The restrictions are also threatening to derail major investment projects.

Bankers have frozen work on a $480m (£366m) loan to Singapore-based Aolani Cloud, which planned to buy Nvidia chips for a Malaysian data centre serving ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok.

The Financial Times reported that ByteDance was now considering abandoning the arrangement altogether.

The news follows weeks of turmoil at Nvidia, caused by Mr Huang's affair with a suspected China spy, which led to his initial resignation from the business.
